Let \( A_1, A_2, A_3, \ldots \) be a sequence of finite nonempty sets of positive integers. Given that \( |A_i \cap A_j| = \gcd(i, j) \) for all (not necessarily distinct) positive integers \( i \) and \( j \), compute the minimum possible value of

\[
\sum_{d|250} \max A_d,
\]

where the sum ranges over all positive integer divisors \( d \) of 250.

(For a finite nonempty set \( S \), we define \( \max S \) as the largest element of \( S \).)

Let \(\varphi\) denote Euler’s totient function.

We first determine the forced structure of the sets \(A_i\).

## 1. The structure of the sets

Taking \(i=j\) gives
\[
|A_i|=i.
\]
Also, if \(j\mid i\), then
\[
|A_i\cap A_j|=\gcd(i,j)=j=|A_j|,
\]
so
\[
A_j\subseteq A_i.
\]

For each positive integer \(n\), define
\[
C_n=A_n\setminus \bigcup_{\substack{d\mid n\\ d<n}} A_d.
\]
We claim that
\[
|C_n|=\varphi(n),
\]
and that for any positive integer \(m\),
\[
C_n\subseteq A_m \iff n\mid m.
\]

This is proved by induction on \(n\). For \(n=1\), \(A_1\) has one element and is contained in every \(A_m\), so \(C_1=A_1\).

Assume the claim holds for all proper divisors of \(n\). Since every proper divisor \(d\mid n\) satisfies \(A_d\subseteq A_n\),
\[
\bigcup_{\substack{d\mid n\\ d<n}} A_d
=
\bigcup_{\substack{r\mid n\\ r<n}} C_r.
\]
The sets \(C_r\) for \(r<n\) are disjoint, and by induction
\[
\left|\bigcup_{\substack{r\mid n\\ r<n}} C_r\right|
=
\sum_{\substack{r\mid n\\ r<n}}\varphi(r)
=
n-\varphi(n).
\]
Hence
\[
|C_n|=|A_n|-|A_n\cap\bigcup_{\substack{d\mid n\\d<n}}A_d|
=
n-(n-\varphi(n))
=
\varphi(n).
\]

Now take \(x\in C_n\). If \(n\mid m\), then \(A_n\subseteq A_m\), so \(x\in A_m\). If \(n\nmid m\), let \(g=\gcd(n,m)\). Then \(g<n\), and by induction
\[
A_g\subseteq A_n\cap A_m,
\]
with
\[
|A_g|=g=|A_n\cap A_m|.
\]
Thus \(A_n\cap A_m=A_g\). But \(x\notin A_g\), because \(g\) is a proper divisor of \(n\). Therefore \(x\notin A_m\). This proves the claim.

Consequently,
\[
A_m=\bigsqcup_{n\mid m} C_n,
\]
with \(|C_n|=\varphi(n)\).

For our problem, the only classes that appear in \(A_d\) with \(d\mid 250\) are
\[
C_1,C_2,C_5,C_{10},C_{25},C_{50},C_{125},C_{250}.
\]
Their sizes are
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
n & 1 & 2 & 5 & 10 & 25 & 50 & 125 & 250\\ \hline
\varphi(n) & 1 & 1 & 4 & 4 & 20 & 20 & 100 & 100
\end{array}
\]
and these add to \(250\).

## 2. Reducing to a labeling/ordering problem

Only the elements in the eight classes above affect the required sum. In an optimal labeling, those \(250\) elements may be assumed to be exactly
\[
1,2,\dots,250.
\]
Indeed, replacing each of them by its rank among the \(250\) elements can only decrease all maxima.

For a class \(C_n\), let \(m_n\) be its largest label. Then for \(d\mid 250\),
\[
\max A_d=\max_{n\mid d} m_n.
\]

Now suppose the eight classes are ordered by increasing maxima:
\[
c_1,c_2,\dots,c_8.
\]
Let
\[
P_k=\sum_{j=1}^k \varphi(c_j).
\]
Because the first \(k\) classes all have labels at most \(m_{c_k}\), we must have
\[
P_k\le m_{c_k}.
\]
If we relabel class \(C_{c_k}\) by the consecutive block
\[
P_{k-1}+1,\dots,P_k,
\]
then its maximum becomes \(P_k\le m_{c_k}\), and no \(\max A_d\) can increase. Therefore an optimal assignment exists in which the classes occupy consecutive blocks in some order.

Thus the problem becomes: order the eight divisors
\[
1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250
\]
so that if \(P_k\) is the prefix sum of \(\varphi\)-sizes, then
\[
\sum_{d\mid 250} \max_{\substack{k\\ c_k\mid d}} P_k
\]
is minimized.

## 3. Finding the optimal order

We determine the optimal order from the largest labels downward.

For a set \(S\) of classes, let
\[
p(S)=\sum_{n\in S}\varphi(n).
\]
If the last class in an ordering of \(S\) is \(x\), then every divisor \(d\mid 250\) whose required classes are all inside \(S\) and which contains \(x\) has maximum \(p(S)\). The remaining divisors are handled by \(S\setminus\{x\}\).

The following table gives the optimal backward choices.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
S & p(S) & \text{active }d\text{'s} & \text{optimal last class} & F(S)\\ \hline
\{1\} & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\\
\{1,2\} & 2 & 1,2 & 2 & 3\\
\{1,2,5\} & 6 & 1,2,5 & 5 & 9\\
\{1,2,5,10\} & 10 & 1,2,5,10 & 10 & 19\\
\{1,2,5,10,25\} & 30 & 1,2,5,10,25 & 25 & 49\\
\{1,2,5,10,25,50\} & 50 & 1,2,5,10,25,50 & 50 & 99\\
\{1,2,5,10,25,50,125\} & 150 & 1,2,5,10,25,50,125 & 125 & 249\\
\{1,2,5,10,25,50,125,250\} & 250 & \text{all eight} & 250 & 499
\end{array}
\]

A few justifications of the nontrivial rows:

- For \(S=\{1,2,5\}\), putting \(5\) last gives
  \[
  6+F(\{1,2\})=6+3=9.
  \]
  Putting \(2\) last gives at least
  \[
  6+(1+5)=12,
  \]
  and putting \(1\) last gives \(18\). So the optimum is \(9\).

- For \(S=\{1,2,5,10,25\}\), putting \(25\) last gives
  \[
  30+F(\{1,2,5,10\})=30+19=49.
  \]
  If \(10\) were last, the remaining active sets have sizes \(1,2,5,25\), so their maxima sum to at least \(33\), giving total at least \(63\). Other choices give an immediate contribution of at least \(60\).

- For \(S=\{1,2,5,10,25,50,125\}\), putting \(125\) last gives
  \[
  150+F(\{1,2,5,10,25,50\})=150+99=249.
  \]
  If \(50\) were last, the remaining active sets include one of size \(125\) and one of size \(1\), contributing at least \(126\), so the total is at least \(276\). Any other last class appears in at least two active sets, giving immediate contribution at least \(300\).

- For the full set, only \(C_{250}\) appears in exactly one of the eight sets \(A_d\). If any other class were last, at least two of the eight maxima would equal \(250\), giving total at least \(500>499\). Thus \(250\) must be last.

Therefore the minimum possible sum is \(499\).

## 4. Construction attaining the bound

Take the order
\[
1,\;2,\;5,\;10,\;25,\;50,\;125,\;250
\]
and assign consecutive labels:
\[
\begin{aligned}
C_1&=\{1\},\\
C_2&=\{2\},\\
C_5&=\{3,4,5,6\},\\
C_{10}&=\{7,8,9,10\},\\
C_{25}&=\{11,\dots,30\},\\
C_{50}&=\{31,\dots,50\},\\
C_{125}&=\{51,\dots,150\},\\
C_{250}&=\{151,\dots,250\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For classes not dividing \(250\), assign any unused labels larger than \(250\).

Then the maxima are
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
d & 1 & 2 & 5 & 10 & 25 & 50 & 125 & 250\\ \hline
\max A_d & 1 & 2 & 6 & 10 & 30 & 50 & 150 & 250
\end{array}
\]
and
\[
1+2+6+10+30+50+150+250=499.
\]

Thus the minimum possible value is

\[
\boxed{499}
\]
